title: A story told beside a fire
hookLine: the Mahabharata begins with a king's fire for snakes, and the whole epic is told to him beside it
carry: itihasa: dharma learned from what happened

last: TAT TVAM ASI: THAT YOU ARE.

lines: A FOREST, A SACRIFICE, A VISITOR.
A STORY HEARD AT A KING'S FIRE.
cards: A forest called Naimisha. The sage Shaunaka and his companions are keeping a twelve-year sacrifice there. A traveler arrives: Ugrashravas, known as Sauti, the son of the storyteller Lomaharshana.

They make him welcome and ask what anyone asks a visitor: where have you come from? From the snake sacrifice of King Janamejaya, he says, where he heard a great story told from beginning to end. The sages want all of it.
So year three opens the way the Mahabharata opens: not on a battlefield, but in a forest, with someone asking for a story.

teach.b: This is the Adi Parva, the opening book of the Mahabharata, which year three follows a piece at a time, in Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English. Before a single hero appears, it builds a frame.
Sauti heard the story at King Janamejaya's sacrifice, told by Vaishampayana, a disciple of Vyasa; and Vyasa, the text says, composed the poem. Hand to hand, and now, through the book, to you.
Janamejaya is the great-grandson of Arjuna, one of the Pandava brothers.
His father, King Parikshit, died from the bite of Takshaka, a king of the snakes.

So Janamejaya lit a great fire meant to draw every snake into the flames, and beside that fire, his family's whole war was told to him. That's why the greatest war story starts with snakes. Here's the teaching.

The Mahabharata calls itself itihasa, usually explained as so indeed it was: not a rulebook, not a fairy tale, but what happened, told so you can watch dharma being kept and broken by real-seeming people.
It even boasts, in its first book, about dharma, wealth, love and freedom: what is here may be found elsewhere; what is not here is found nowhere.
And Hindus have mostly met it the way Janamejaya did: by hearing it, from a grandparent, a reciter, a TV serial, a teacher.
Some readers hear the frame as a question the poem asks itself: what does a man in the middle of vengeance need to hear?
Its answer is the story of where vengeance leads.

how: In many Hindu homes and temples the Mahabharata is heard more than read: a reciter or grandparent tells it in parts over many evenings, explaining as they go, and many families first met it through the televised serial. This year follows Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English translation, which is in the public domain.

games.q: your little cousin asks why your family tells the Mahabharata out loud instead of just teaching the rules. what fits?

games.why: the whole epic is told to a king beside his revenge fire. dharma is learned by hearing what people did, and what came of it.

practice: The Mahabharata opens with a bow: to Narayana, to Nara, and to Sarasvati, goddess of learning and speech, before the story is spoken. If you pray, make that small bow now, in your own words.

Then just listen, to the room and the breath, for the rest of the sit. In Hindu learning, hearing, shravana, comes first. If you don't pray, bow your head to whoever first told you a story that mattered, and listen.
